title: Don't believe every word (I.4)
hook: a rumor lands in the family group chat; chapter four of the Imitation says weigh what you hear before you believe or pass it on
tomorrow: fancy old words or a plain Bible: which one tells the truth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one bite settled what every review couldn't: happy is the one truth itself teaches, with a good life first. The line was truth itself teaches.

A message lands in the family group chat. Somebody's cousin heard the parish is closing, the priest is leaving, and someone's in trouble. A shocked face. A crying face. One person forwards it to another chat. Nobody asks where it came from. A thumb hovers over the forward button. Chapter four of The Imitation of Christ was written for that thumb. Its first move is a single verb you can feel in your hands: weigh it.
screen: `THE PARISH IS CLOSING?` → `ONE FORWARD, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE THUMB, HOVERING.`

segments.voice: Don't believe every word or every impulse, the chapter says. A matter should be weighed carefully and patiently, before God. Then it names the reason, and it's honest about us. People believe and speak evil of others more readily than good, it says, so weak are we. The wise don't easily credit every tale, because they know how human talk slides toward the worst version. So the chapter gives a double piece of wisdom, and the second half is easy to skip. Don't believe everything you hear. And don't rush to pass on what you've heard. Both. Checking isn't enough if you forward it anyway. It leans on an older book of the Bible, the one the Douay-Rheims calls Ecclesiasticus, also known as Sirach, which says that someone quick to believe is light of heart. And it closes with a practical move: take counsel from someone wise and conscientious, rather than following your own guess. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: a spiritual classic about following Christ stops, in chapter four, to talk about gossip. Because what we believe about each other shapes how we treat each other.
screen: `WEIGH IT, BEFORE GOD.` · `EVIL BELIEVED FASTER THAN GOOD.` · `DON'T BELIEVE IT, DON'T PASS IT ON.` · `ASK SOMEONE WISE.` · then, large: `WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: Hold two things, one in each hand: a phone and a cup, a book and a set of keys. Don't guess from how they look; feel slowly which one is heavier, until you're sure. That patience in your hands is the chapter's word for what you hear.
Don't believe every word. Chapter four's counsel: weigh what you hear patiently, and don't rush to repeat it.
Your line: weigh it. Two hands and one pause, before anything gets forwarded anywhere. Sleep well.

howItsDone: The Catechism counts rash judgment and detraction, believing or spreading harm about others without cause, as sins against the truth; Catholics bring these to confession and try to interpret others' words in the best light.

chat.says: back from the oregon visit, loved it. now a teammate says their coach is leaving. panic?
options: Weigh it first. Ask where it came from, and check before you believe or repeat it.
Panic a little. Bad news usually turns out true, so plan like he's already gone.
Ignore it. Nobody's word can be trusted, so there's no point in checking.

The Imitation of Christ.meaning: a short book of counsel credited to Thomas à Kempis

Ecclesiasticus.meaning: a Bible book of wisdom sayings, in Catholic Bibles

Sirach.meaning: another name for Ecclesiasticus, after its author

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English Bible translation

sources.work: The Imitation of Christ (attributed to Thomas à Kempis)

notes: Imitation I.4 paraphrased: do not believe every word or impulse, but weigh the matter carefully and patiently according to God; we often believe and speak evil of others more readily than good, so weak are we; the perfect do not easily credit every tale, knowing human frailty prone to evil and slippery in words; great wisdom not to be rash in action nor obstinate in opinion, not to believe everything one hears nor straightway to pour into others' ears what one has heard; take counsel of a wise and conscientious man. Confirm.
Sirach 19:4 paraphrased ('he that is hasty to give credit is light of heart'); the Imitation's echo of it is commonly noted. Confirm.
howItsDone: CCC 2477–2478 (rash judgment, detraction; interpreting others favorably) paraphrased; confirm paragraphs.
Gloss 'Sirach ... after its author': the book is attributed to Jesus son of Sirach (Sirach 50:27/29 in some numberings). Confirm.
Latin 'Non est credendum omni verbo nec instinctui' (I.4.1): confirm.
